title: Scope, client approval and exclusions
audience: Garden maintenance and clean-up workers, crew leaders and the people who take bookings and quote garden jobs.
learningOutcomes: Describe the scope of a garden clean-up using the client's written request, the site walk and the agreed boundaries.
Identify exclusions, including tree work above a set height or near power lines, and explain why they are excluded.
Handle a client request that goes beyond the agreed scope by pausing work and getting written approval.
Record the scope, access, exclusions and any variation so that the job can be verified at handover.

instruction.heading: What a garden scope is and why it matters
instruction.body: A garden clean-up looks simple until the crew reaches the back fence. A client may ask for the whole yard to be cleared, but the boundary might include a neighbour's tree, a garden bed the client has forgotten, an irrigation valve under the leaves or a protected plant. The scope is the written statement of what will be done, where, how far, with what waste removal and within what time. It turns a vague request into a job everyone can check. Without a clear scope, workers make decisions on the spot, clients expect results you did not agree to, and disputes about cost and damage follow. Your first job on any garden site is to compare what the client asked for with what the written scope says, and to ask for clarification before cutting anything you cannot confidently identify or are not authorised to touch. Use {{business:services.service_description}} as the reference for what the business normally offers, and record any difference from the standard service.

instruction.heading: Boundaries, access and protected items
instruction.body: Walk the boundary with the client before work starts. Identify the property line, any shared fences, easements, paths and areas that belong to a neighbour or to a public authority. Note the garden beds, lawns, planted areas and structures that are inside the scope and those that are outside it. Ask about protected or sensitive plantings, such as heritage-listed trees, specimen plants, native vegetation and any vegetation that the client or council has told you not to disturb. Where a planting is unidentified, treat it as protected until the client confirms otherwise. Record access arrangements, including gates, pets, working hours, water and power supply, and the places where material may be stored or staged. Photograph the agreed boundary and the disputed areas with the client's permission and label the exclusions on the photograph. If a neighbour's property is affected, do not work on it without the owner's written permission.

instruction.heading: Exclusions and licensed work
instruction.body: Exclusions are work you agree not to do. They are as important as the inclusions. Typical exclusions for a garden clean-up include: work on structures; irrigation and electrical repairs; removal of large stumps; pesticide or herbicide application unless the business holds the licence or authority that applies at that location; and tree work. In New South Wales, the EPA's 2018 fact sheet says that people who spray weeds commercially need a ground-applicator licence. Tree work near power lines is excluded from this business. Council tree rules decide whether a tree needs a permit, and they differ between councils: one NSW council exempts trees under five metres from its permit rule (no date shown), while Brisbane requires a permit ahead of working on protected vegetation that is not exempt (no date shown). This lesson does not grant any licence. If a client asks for a tree to be felled, lopped above a council threshold or cut back near a power line, record the request, state the exclusion in writing, and refer the client to a suitably licensed arborist. Do not begin any part of that work, including preparation, and do not promise that the business will do it later under the same job.

instruction.heading: Variations, approval and handover
instruction.body: Clients change their minds. A new request for extra cutting, a larger skip, or a different area is a variation. A variation is valid only after the client approves it in writing, for example by message or signed job update, and only once the price and time change is recorded. Stop the work that depends on the variation until approval is in place. Keep the variation with the original scope so that the final inspection can compare what was agreed with what was done. At handover, walk the site with the client and point out the completed areas, the exclusions and any remaining issues. Explain why any excluded item was not touched. A clear record of scope, approval and exclusions protects the client, the business and the crew.

procedure: Read the written request and the job scope, and note any words that are unclear, such as clear, tidy or full clean-up.
Walk the site with the client, marking the boundary, access points, areas to be cut or cleared, and areas to be excluded.
Identify each planting in the scope. Treat any unidentified or possibly protected item as excluded until the client confirms.
Identify exclusions, including tree work above a set height or near power lines, and record each one in writing.
Photograph the agreed boundary and any disputed area with consent, and label the exclusions.
Confirm the scope in writing with the client before work starts, including access, waste removal and the time window.
If the client asks for work outside the scope, stop that item, explain the exclusion and obtain written approval for any variation.
At handover, compare the completed work with the approved scope and record each exclusion and any variation.

workedExamples.situation: A resident asks for a full clearance of the back garden. On the walk-through, the boundary includes a tree the client says is protected and an unlabelled garden bed of unknown plants.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is included in the scope, and what do you say to the client?
workedExamples.reasoning: Include the clearance of the labelled areas that the client confirms are in scope. Exclude the protected tree and the unlabelled bed until the client confirms what they are and whether they can be disturbed. Photograph the areas with consent, label them on the scope sheet and request written clarification. Do not start the tree or the bed. Tell the client that tree work near power lines is outside this business, and that a council permit may be needed for the tree.

workedExamples.situation: Halfway through a clean-up, the client asks the crew to also cut back a large branch that hangs over the neighbour's carport.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the crew do the work on the spot, and what must happen?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The branch is part of a tree, reaches over a neighbour's property and may be above the height or near a line that requires a licence. Stop, explain that the work is outside the scope, and record the request. The client can seek a licensed arborist. Any variation for other garden work needs written approval and a changed scope before work starts.

equipmentAndPpe: Printed or digital scope sheet with boundary map
Camera or phone for recording the boundary, with consent
High-visibility clothing where the site requires it
Gloves and eye protection suitable for the planned clean-up

commonErrors.error: Starting the clean-up on the verbal request, without a written scope.
commonErrors.prevention: Confirm the scope in writing before work starts, including exclusions and access.

commonErrors.error: Removing an unidentified plant because it looks untidy.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat unknown plants as excluded until the client confirms their identity and that they may be removed.

commonErrors.error: Doing a tree cut that the client asked for on the day, because it seemed small.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the request, state the exclusion and refer the client to a licensed arborist. Do not start any part of the tree work.

commonErrors.error: Treating a verbal instruction from the client as a variation.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, record the change and obtain written approval before doing the extra work.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Tree work near power lines is excluded from this business. Whether a tree needs a council permit depends on that council's rules.
This lesson does not grant a tree-work licence, an arborist licence or any authority to work near power lines.
Work on neighbouring property requires the owner's permission.

The model WHS framework requires the business to manage risks from work, including the risk of working in unsafe areas, to the level that is reasonably practicable. A scope that excludes unsafe work is part of that management.

qualityStandard: A written scope, signed or confirmed by the client, is in place before any work starts.
All exclusions, including tree work and any unidentified or protected plantings, are recorded.
Each variation has written client approval before the extra work begins.
The handover record compares the completed work with the approved scope.
documentationEvidence: Scope sheet with boundary map, access notes and the agreed inclusions.
Exclusion record listing each excluded item and the reason.
Written client approval for any variation, with the date and the changed price or time.
Photographs of the boundary and disputed areas taken with consent.
summary: The written scope, agreed with the client, is the reference for what is done and what is not.
Identify exclusions early, especially tree work above a set height or near power lines, and refer them to a licence holder.
Pause and get written approval before any variation.
Compare the completed work with the approved scope at handover.

knowledgeChecks.question: Before starting a garden clean-up, what should the crew do with a plant they cannot identify?
options: Treat it as excluded until the client confirms its identity and that it may be disturbed.
Remove it, because untidy plants are part of a clean-up and the client expects them gone
Cut it back to the ground so the client can see the area clearly from the path

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks for a large branch to be cut back over a neighbour's carport. What is the correct response?
options: Cut it back at the end of the day, since the crew is already on site and the branch is close to the carport roof
Record the request, state that tree work above a set height or near a line is excluded, and refer the client to a licensed arborist.
Agree to do it at a lower price if the client pays cash on the day, which keeps the job simple and quick to finish

knowledgeChecks.question: The client asks for an extra area to be cleared during the job. What must happen before the crew starts that work?
options: The crew starts, and the price is agreed at the end of the job once the total time and the materials are known
The supervisor approves the change verbally on the phone, and the crew notes it on the sheet for the job
The variation is recorded and approved in writing, with any price and time change, before the extra work begins.
